claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017.

claims.claim: RSV replicates in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Like all pneumoviruses, RSV replicates in the cytoplasm (Collins et al., 2013), but specific interaction with host cell organelles, and the mitochondria in particular, has remained largely unexplored.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2013.

claims.claim: RSV infection impacts the abundance of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins.
claims.source: Unbiased discovery studies capitalising on quantitative proteomic protocols to identify changes in protein levels upon RSV infection have revealed a significant impact on the abundance of a number of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015), including respiratory complex I proteins, outer mitochondrial membrane complex subunits, voltage-dependent anion channel protein, and the prohibitin subunits that play essential roles in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics, morphology and biogenesis (Kipper et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015.

claims.claim: RSV infection affects respiratory complex I proteins.
claims.source: Unbiased discovery studies capitalising on quantitative proteomic protocols to identify changes in protein levels upon RSV infection have revealed a significant impact on the abundance of a number of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015), including respiratory complex I proteins, outer mitochondrial membrane complex subunits, voltage-dependent anion channel protein, and the prohibitin subunits that play essential roles in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics, morphology and biogenesis (Kipper et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claims.claim: Oxidative phosphorylation is responsible for up to 90% of cellular ATP production.
claims.source: Oxidative phosphorylation driven by ATP synthase/complex V and the electron transport chain (complexes I-IV) is responsible for up to 90% of cellular ATP production (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016.

claims.claim: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions.
claims.source: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016), but oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity (Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity.
claims.source: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016), but oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity (Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014.

claims.claim: Mitochondria are trafficked intracellularly through the action of molecular motors operating on microtubules and actin filaments.
claims.source: Changes in cytoskeletal organization and/or motor activities can impact mitochondrial distribution and function because mitochondria are trafficked intracellularly through the action of molecular motors operating on microtubules and actin filaments (Welte, 2004; Hancock, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Welte, 2004; Hancock, 2014.

claims.claim: RSV infection results in a higher percentage of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology compared to uninfected cells.
claims.source: Mock- and RSV-infected cells exhibited fragmented, tubular and fibrillar morphologies as revealed by MitoTrackerRed staining (Figure 1A), with a higher percentage of infected cells showing fragmented morphology, and a lower percentage with tubular and fibrillar morphologies, compared to uninfected cells (Hu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows quantification demonstrating a significant >30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology following infection.

claims.claim: RSV infection results in a lower percentage of cells with tubular and fibrillar mitochondrial morphologies compared to uninfected cells.
claims.source: Mock- and RSV-infected cells exhibited fragmented, tubular and fibrillar morphologies as revealed by MitoTrackerRed staining (Figure 1A), with a higher percentage of infected cells showing fragmented morphology, and a lower percentage with tubular and fibrillar morphologies, compared to uninfected cells (Hu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows quantification of mitochondrial morphologies with decreased tubular and fibrillar percentages in RSV-infected cells.

claims.claim: RSV infection causes a significant >30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology at 8 h p.i.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis confirmed the observations, with a significant (p<0.001)>30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology following infection, compared to mock infected cells (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows quantitative data with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: The Golgi apparatus remains asymmetrically close to the nuclei in both mock- and RSV-infected cells.
claims.source: To confirm that the effects on host mitochondria are specific, we also tested for changes in the Golgi apparatus by staining using the CellLight Golgi-GFP *BacMam 2.0* (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The Golgi cisterna remained asymmetrically close to the nuclei in mock- and RSV-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in stark contrast to the striking changes in mitochondria at 8 and 24 h p.i.
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows Golgi staining that does not change with RSV infection, serving as a control.

claims.claim: RSV infection specifically reorganizes host cell mitochondria with perinuclear clustering followed by MTOC-oriented asymmetry.
claims.source: Together, these findings indicate that RSV infection specifically reorganizes the host cell mitochondria, with perinuclear clustering followed by MTOC-oriented asymmetry.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the imaging data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: RSV induces perinuclear mitochondrial clustering in human airway basal cells (BCi-NS1).
claims.source: BCi-NS1 cells were infected with RSV for 18 or 36 h p.i. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). In contrast to the even distribution of mitochondria throughout the mock-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; first two rows), substantial perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 36 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; 3rd and 4th rows), completely consistent with our observations in A549 cells (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows imaging and quantitative analysis in BCi-NS1 cells demonstrating perinuclear clustering.

claims.claim: R90% is significantly reduced by over 30% in RSV-infected BCi-NS1 cells at 18 or 36 h p.i. compared to mock-infected cells.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis of the R90% parameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) confirmed these observations, whereby R90% was significantly (p<0.01) reduced (over 30%) in RSV-infected cells at 18 or 36 h p.i., compared to mock-infected cells.
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B shows quantitative data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network.
claims.source: Significantly, RSV-infected cells continued to show perinuclear clustering of mitochondria following treatment with cytochalasin D (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C) but not with nocodazole (Figure 3A, Figure 3 - Figure 1—video 3), confirming that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network but not the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: Figure 3A and 3B show that nocodazole treatment prevents mitochondrial clustering while cytochalasin D does not.

claims.claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is not dependent on the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: Significantly, RSV-infected cells continued to show perinuclear clustering of mitochondria following treatment with cytochalasin D (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C) but not with nocodazole (Figure 3A, Figure 3 - Figure 1—video 3), confirming that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network but not the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows that cytochalasin D treatment does not prevent mitochondrial clustering.

claims.claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering relies on dynein-dependent retrograde transport along intact microtubules.
claims.source: Strikingly, RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering was completely abolished by treatment with EHNA but not monastrol. Quantitative analysis for the R90% parameter confirmed this finding (Figure 3B), indicating that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering relies on dynein-dependent retrograde transport along intact microtubules.
claims.evidence: Figure 3A and 3B show that EHNA (dynein inhibitor) prevents clustering while monastrol (kinesin inhibitor) does not.

claims.claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is suppressed by depletion of DYNLT1.
claims.source: Consistent with the effects for EHNA above, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was suppressed by depletion of either DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1, resulting in an even distribution of reticular mitochondria (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of DYNLT1 prevents mitochondrial clustering.

claims.claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is suppressed by depletion of DYNC1H1.
claims.source: Consistent with the effects for EHNA above, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was suppressed by depletion of either DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1, resulting in an even distribution of reticular mitochondria (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of DYNC1H1 prevents mitochondrial clustering.

claims.claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is not affected by depletion of KLC1.
claims.source: In contrast, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was not affected by depletion of KLC1 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of KLC1 does not prevent mitochondrial clustering.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry at 18 hr RSV infection.
claims.source: We extended our analysis to the RSV-induced mitochondrial asymmetry that follows mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, finding that nocodazole and EHNA treatments prevent the MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry characteristic of longer (18 hr) RSV infection (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C show that nocodazole treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial distribution.

claims.claim: EHNA treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry at 18 hr RSV infection.
claims.source: We extended our analysis to the RSV-induced mitochondrial asymmetry that follows mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, finding that nocodazole and EHNA treatments prevent the MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry characteristic of longer (18 hr) RSV infection (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C show that EHNA treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial distribution.

claims.claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial redistribution is dynein/microtubule-dependent.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis for the angular mitochondrial distribution (Figure 4B–4C) supported this conclusion, results overall demonstrating a dynein/microtubule-dependent mechanism underlying RSV-induced mitochondrial redistribution during the course of infection.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figures 3 and 4 showing effects of microtubule and dynein inhibition.

claims.claim: OCR progressively decreases during RSV infection from 6-24 hr.
claims.source: We used the Seahorse XF96 Extracellular Flux Analyser to measure oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) of living cells over the time course (6–24 hr) of RSV infection (Figure 5A), as indicators of mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis, respectively (Wu et al., 2007). OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
claims.evidence: Figure 5A shows Seahorse bioenergetics data demonstrating progressive decrease in OCR over time.

claims.claim: ECAR increases during RSV infection from 6-24 hr.
claims.source: OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
claims.evidence: Figure 5A inset shows correlation of OCR and ECAR with ECAR increasing as OCR decreases.

claims.claim: RSV infection inhibits mitochondrial respiration and increases glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
claims.source: OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the OCR and ECAR data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Increasing multiplicity of infection (MOI) results in more severe effects on mitochondrial respiration.
claims.source: These effects paralleled the robustness of infection, with increasing multiplicity of infection (MOI) resulting in more severe effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1C show dose-dependent effects of RSV MOI on respiratory parameters.

claims.claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in maximal OCR from 8 h p.i.
claims.source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in basal OCR from 18 h p.i.
claims.source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in ATP-linked OCR from 18 h p.i.
claims.source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: RSV infection causes significant increases in non-mitochondrial OCR from 8 h p.i.
claims.source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment restores all respiratory activities in RSV-infected cells at 18 h p.i.
claims.source: Strikingly, all respiratory activities (basal, ATP-linked, maximal and non-mitochondrial) in the RSV-infected cells treated with nocodazole or EHNA remained unchanged (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows that nocodazole treatment prevents RSV-induced changes in respiratory parameters.

claims.claim: EHNA treatment restores all respiratory activities in RSV-infected cells at 18 h p.i.
claims.source: Strikingly, all respiratory activities (basal, ATP-linked, maximal and non-mitochondrial) in the RSV-infected cells treated with nocodazole or EHNA remained unchanged (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows that EHNA treatment prevents RSV-induced changes in respiratory parameters.

claims.claim: RSV-induced changes in host cell respiration activities are dependent on dynein/microtubules.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the RSV-induced changes in host cell respiration activities are dependent on dynein/microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 5C showing that inhibiting microtubules or dynein prevents respiratory changes.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial respiration is required to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm.
claims.source: Mitochondrial respiration is required to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm (Gottlieb et al., 2003; Dey and Moraes, 2000).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gottlieb et al., 2003; Dey and Moraes, 2000.

claims.claim: RSV infection induces a loss of host cell mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm by ~18 h p.i.
claims.source: Thus, by ~18 h p.i., RSV infection induces a loss of host cell mitochondrial membrane potential, Δψm.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the TMRE and TPE-Ph-In imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Lower TMRE fluorescence is observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 24 h p.i.
claims.source: Lower TMRE fluorescence was observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 24 h p.i., an impact strikingly apparent when infected cells were imaged alongside non-infected cells in the same field (Figure 6A, 5th and 6th rows of panels).
claims.evidence: Figure 6A shows live cell imaging with TMRE demonstrating reduced fluorescence in infected cells.

claims.claim: Δψm is significantly reduced at 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells.
claims.source: Quantification of the integrated density of TMRE fluorescence confirmed the results, revealing significantly reduced (p<0.001) Δψm at 18 h p.i. (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Figure 6B shows quantification of TMRE fluorescence with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: TPE-Ph-In fluorescence shows progressive loss from 16 to 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells.
claims.source: To monitor these RSV-induced changes in Δψm over the period of 16–18 h p.i. in real time, we used the photobleach-resistant Δψm-sensitive dye tetraphenylethylene-phenyl-indolium salt (TPE-Ph-In) (Zhao et al., 2015), documenting that TPE-Ph-In fluorescence was maintained throughout the 2 hr imaging period in mock-infected cells, but showed a progressive loss of TPE-Ph-In fluorescence at 16 to 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows time-lapse imaging with TPE-Ph-In demonstrating progressive loss of signal in infected cells.

claims.claim: RSV infection increases mitochondrial ROS generation significantly by 18 h p.i.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis of the ratiometric images highlighted the extent of ROS production (Figure 7B), with the results indicating that RSV infection increases mitochondrial ROS generation significantly (p<0.001) by 18 h p.i.
claims.evidence: Figure 7B shows quantification of FRR2 ratiometric imaging with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: MitoQ suppresses rotenone-induced mitochondrial ROS production.
claims.source: We treated mock-infected cells with rotenone as a positive control, with strong FRR2 emission in regions colocalizing with Mitotracker Deep Red (Figure 7A, 3rd row of panels), indicative of high levels of mitochondrial ROS. To confirm the mitochondrial contribution to this staining, we used the mitochondrial ROS scavenger mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) (Smith and Murphy, 2010; Maharjan et al., 2014), which strongly suppresses the actions of rotenone (Figure 7A, 4th row of panels).
claims.evidence: Figure 7A shows that MitoQ treatment reduces FRR2 signal in rotenone-treated cells.

claims.claim: MitoQ reduces RSV-induced mitochondrial ROS production.
claims.source: FRR2 fluorescence increased in RSV-infected cells, but was also reduced by MitoQ (Figure 7A; bottom 4 rows of panels).
claims.evidence: Figure 7A and 7B show that MitoQ treatment reduces FRR2 signal in RSV-infected cells.

claims.claim: RSV infection increases population 1 (high ROS) cells by about 2-fold at 8 hr and 8-fold at 18 hr compared to mock infection.
claims.source: Compared to mock infection, RSV infection at 8 and 18 hr increased population 1 by about 2- and 8-fold, respectively, with these increases reversed by MitoQ (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Figure 7C shows FACS analysis quantifying populations with high and low ROS.

claims.claim: MitoQ reverses RSV-induced increases in high ROS cell populations.
claims.source: Compared to mock infection, RSV infection at 8 and 18 hr increased population 1 by about 2- and 8-fold, respectively, with these increases reversed by MitoQ (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Figure 7C shows FACS analysis demonstrating MitoQ reduces the high ROS population in infected cells.

claims.claim: Higher levels of ROS are associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.
claims.source: Analysis of RSV-infected cells revealed higher levels of ROS associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.; this staining at 12 h p.i. was still perinuclear, but with intense nuclear staining as well as some diffuse cytoplasmic staining (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Figure 7D shows DCF staining colocalizing with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.

claims.claim: At 12 h p.i., ROS staining is perinuclear with intense nuclear staining and some diffuse cytoplasmic staining.
claims.source: Analysis of RSV-infected cells revealed higher levels of ROS associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.; this staining at 12 h p.i. was still perinuclear, but with intense nuclear staining as well as some diffuse cytoplasmic staining (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Figure 7D shows DCF staining pattern at 12 h p.i.

claims.claim: MitoQ markedly reduces DCF staining in RSV-infected cells.
claims.source: We then treated RSV-infected cells with MitoQ 2 hr before imaging and observed a marked reduction in DCF staining, suggesting that the ROS generated in the absence of MitoQ in infected cells was largely mitochondrial (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Figure 7D shows reduced DCF staining with MitoQ treatment in infected cells.

claims.claim: ROS generated in RSV-infected cells is largely mitochondrial.
claims.source: We then treated RSV-infected cells with MitoQ 2 hr before imaging and observed a marked reduction in DCF staining, suggesting that the ROS generated in the absence of MitoQ in infected cells was largely mitochondrial (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the fact that MitoQ, a mitochondria-specific ROS scavenger, reduces DCF staining.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment prevents nuclear accumulation of ROS in RSV-infected cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, when we included nocodazole treatment to prevent microtubule-dependent mitochondrial clustering upon RSV infection, DCF staining remained largely mitochondrial and cytoplasmic and was largely excluded from the nucleus (Figure 7D, bottom row).
claims.evidence: Figure 7D shows that nocodazole treatment changes the pattern of DCF staining, keeping it cytoplasmic rather than nuclear.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial perinuclear redistribution is a prerequisite for altering the oxidative status of the host cell nucleus during RSV infection.
claims.source: An implication of these findings is that mitochondrial perinuclear redistribution is a prerequisite for altering the oxidative status of the host cell nucleus during RSV infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that preventing mitochondrial redistribution with nocodazole prevents nuclear ROS accumulation.

claims.claim: Addition of MitoQ at 8 or 18 h p.i. reduces viral genome replication by up to 60% at 24 h p.i.
claims.source: Excitingly, addition of MitoQ at 8 or even 18 h p.i. had a significant (p<0.001) inhibitory effect, reducing viral genome replication by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs measured at 24 h p.i. (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Figure 7E shows qPCR data demonstrating reduced viral RNA copy numbers with MitoQ treatment.

claims.claim: Addition of MitoQ at 8 or 18 h p.i. reduces infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs at 24 h p.i.
claims.source: Excitingly, addition of MitoQ at 8 or even 18 h p.i. had a significant (p<0.001) inhibitory effect, reducing viral genome replication by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs measured at 24 h p.i. (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Figure 7E shows plaque assay data demonstrating reduced infectious virus with MitoQ treatment.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production.
claims.source: These results confirm that mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production, and that MitoQ, as a specific inhibitor of mitochondrial ROS, is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MitoQ inhibition data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: MitoQ is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
claims.source: These results confirm that mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production, and that MitoQ, as a specific inhibitor of mitochondrial ROS, is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MitoQ inhibition data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: MitoQ does not alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i.
claims.source: MitoQ was found not to alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i. (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread to neighboring uninfected cells through cell fusion.
claims.evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1B shows quantification of syncytia with no significant difference with MitoQ treatment.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread through cell fusion.
claims.source: MitoQ was found not to alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i. (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread to neighboring uninfected cells through cell fusion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MitoQ reduces virus production but does not affect syncytia formation.

claims.claim: Microtubule and dynein are necessary for the formation of RSV infectious virus filaments.
claims.source: Previous studies have indicated that microtubule and dynein are necessary for the formation of RSV infectious virus filaments (Vanover et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Vanover et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Treatment with nocodazole significantly reduces infectious virus production by up to 2.5 log.
claims.source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with nocodazole treatment.

claims.claim: Treatment with EHNA significantly reduces infectious virus production by up to 2.5 log.
claims.source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with EHNA treatment.

claims.claim: Cytochalasin D has no significant effect on infectious virus production.
claims.source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with cytochalasin D treatment showing no significant effect.

claims.claim: Monastrol has no significant effect on infectious virus production.
claims.source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with monastrol treatment showing no significant effect.

claims.claim: siRNA-knockdown of DYNLT1 results in significant decreases in infectious virus production (2-3 logs).
claims.source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with DYNLT1 siRNA knockdown.

claims.claim: siRNA-knockdown of DYNC1H1 results in significant decreases in infectious virus production (2-3 logs).
claims.source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with DYNC1H1 siRNA knockdown.

claims.claim: siRNA-knockdown of KLC1 does not result in significant decreases in infectious virus production.
claims.source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with KLC1 siRNA knockdown showing no significant effect.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial reorganization, rather than the microtubule network per se, is key to RSV infection.
claims.source: None of the treatments above impacting mitochondrial distribution induced by RSV infection, apart from nocodazole, impact microtubules directly (see Figure 3AD), implying that mitochondrial redistribution, rather than the microtubule network per se, is key to RSV infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EHNA and dynein siRNAs, which don't affect microtubule structure, still inhibit virus production.

claims.claim: CLUH plays a key role in mitochondrial distribution independent of the microtubule network.
claims.source: To examine this idea further, we performed knockdown experiments for the mRNA-binding protein CLUH (clustered mitochondria homolog) (Figure 8A), which plays a key role in mitochondrial distribution independent of the microtubule network by facilitating translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes close to mitochondria (Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014.

claims.claim: CLUH-targeting siRNA induces mitochondrial perinuclear clustering in mock infected cells.
claims.source: As observed previously (Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014), CLUH-targeting siRNA but not control scrambled siRNA induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering in mock infected cells (Figure 8B; first two rows), with RSV-infection resulting in only a further slight increase in clustering (Figure 8B; 4th row).

results.result: RSV infection induces staged mitochondrial redistribution, with perinuclear clustering at 8-12 h p.i. followed by MTOC-oriented asymmetric distribution at 18-24 h p.i. This was demonstrated in both A549 cells and human airway basal cells (BCi-NS1), with quantitative analysis showing >30% reduction in R90% parameter and increased mitochondrial signal within 45° of the MTOC.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C23-C25, C27-C29, and C130-C133 are well-supported by high-resolution imaging data (Figures 1-2), quantitative analysis of mitochondrial distribution (R90% parameter), and validation in multiple cell types including primary human airway cells. The temporal progression is clearly documented with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001). The Golgi control (C26) confirms specificity of the mitochondrial effects.

results.result: RSV-induced mitochondrial redistribution is dependent on intact microtubules and dynein motor proteins, but not on actin cytoskeleton or kinesin. This was demonstrated through pharmacological inhibition (nocodazole, EHNA vs. cytochalasin D, monastrol) and siRNA knockdown experiments (DYNLT1, DYNC1H1 vs. KLC1).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C38 and C134 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (Figures 3-4). Pharmacological inhibitors show specific effects on mitochondrial clustering and MTOC-oriented asymmetry, with appropriate controls. siRNA knockdown experiments confirm the requirement for dynein components with proper validation of knockdown efficiency (Figure 3C). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of effect with actin/kinesin inhibition.

results.result: RSV infection progressively impairs mitochondrial respiration over 6-24 h p.i., with decreased OCR and increased ECAR indicating a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis. Significant decreases in maximal OCR occur from 8 h p.i., and basal/ATP-linked OCR from 18 h p.i., with effects proportional to MOI.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C39-C46, C103, and C138 are well-supported by Seahorse bioenergetics analysis (Figure 5) showing time-dependent and dose-dependent effects on multiple respiratory parameters. The correlation between OCR and ECAR (R²=0.9745) supports the metabolic shift interpretation. Statistical significance is properly documented (p<0.001 to p<0.05) with appropriate sample sizes (n=3, performed in triplicate).

results.result: Inhibiting microtubule/dynein-dependent mitochondrial redistribution with nocodazole or EHNA restores normal mitochondrial respiratory function in RSV-infected cells, demonstrating that respiratory impairment is dependent on mitochondrial redistribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 and C104 are supported by Seahorse data (Figure 5C) showing that nocodazole and EHNA treatments prevent RSV-induced changes in all respiratory parameters (basal, ATP-linked, maximal, and non-mitochondrial). This establishes a mechanistic link between mitochondrial redistribution and respiratory dysfunction. However, the manuscript does not fully address whether these treatments might have independent effects on mitochondrial function.

results.result: RSV infection causes loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) by ~18 h p.i., demonstrated by reduced TMRE fluorescence and progressive loss of TPE-Ph-In signal during real-time imaging from 16-18 h p.i.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C54, and C139 are supported by multiple complementary approaches using different Δψm-sensitive dyes (Figure 6). TMRE quantification shows significant reduction (p<0.001) at 18 h p.i., and real-time TPE-Ph-In imaging confirms progressive loss. The use of FCCP as a positive control validates the assay. However, the manuscript does not fully address whether Δψm loss is a direct consequence of respiratory impairment or an independent effect.

results.result: RSV infection significantly increases mitochondrial ROS production by 18 h p.i., as demonstrated by FRR2 ratiometric imaging, FACS analysis, and DCF staining. The ROS is largely mitochondrial in origin, as evidenced by MitoQ suppression and colocalization with mitochondrial markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C55-C63, C106, and C140 are well-supported by multiple complementary ROS detection methods (Figure 7). FRR2 ratiometric imaging provides quantitative evidence (p<0.001), FACS analysis shows 2-8 fold increases in high-ROS populations, and DCF staining demonstrates spatial distribution. The mitochondrial origin is confirmed by MitoQ suppression and colocalization with Mitotracker. Rotenone serves as an appropriate positive control.

results.result: Mitochondrial perinuclear redistribution is required for nuclear ROS accumulation during RSV infection, as nocodazole treatment prevents nuclear ROS accumulation while maintaining cytoplasmic/mitochondrial ROS localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by DCF staining experiments (Figure 7D) showing that preventing mitochondrial redistribution with nocodazole changes ROS localization patterns. This establishes a spatial relationship between mitochondrial positioning and nuclear oxidative stress. However, the mechanistic basis for this relationship is not fully elucidated, and the claim about nuclear ROS impacting transcription (C128-C129) remains speculative.

results.result: The mitochondrial ROS scavenger MitoQ potently inhibits RSV infection in cell culture, reducing viral genome replication by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs when added at 8 or 18 h p.i.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C66-C69, C107, and C121 are strongly supported by qPCR and plaque assay data (Figure 7E) showing dose-dependent and time-dependent inhibition of viral replication with statistical significance (p<0.001). The ability to inhibit infection even when added at 18 h p.i. suggests therapeutic potential. The lack of effect on syncytia formation (C70-C71) supports the interpretation that MitoQ affects replication rather than cell-to-cell spread.

results.result: Agents targeting microtubule integrity (nocodazole) or dynein motor function (EHNA, siRNA knockdown of DYNLT1/DYNC1H1) significantly reduce RSV virus production by 2-3 logs, while actin or kinesin inhibition has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C73-C79, C120, and C142-C143 are supported by plaque assay data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) showing specific effects of microtubule/dynein inhibition on virus production with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001 to p<0.05). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of effect with cytochalasin D and monastrol. LDH assays (C87-C89) confirm that effects are not due to cytotoxicity. However, the manuscript acknowledges that nocodazole may have effects beyond mitochondrial redistribution.

results.result: Mitochondrial reorganization per se, rather than microtubule network integrity, is key to RSV infection. CLUH knockdown, which induces mitochondrial clustering independent of microtubules, increases both mitochondrial ROS production and virus production.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 and C135-C137 are supported by CLUH knockdown experiments (Figure 8) showing that inducing mitochondrial clustering through a microtubule-independent mechanism still enhances ROS production (p<0.01) and virus production (p<0.01). This elegant experiment distinguishes between effects on microtubules versus mitochondrial positioning. However, the interpretation relies on the assumption that CLUH acts solely through mitochondrial positioning, which may be an oversimplification given CLUH's role in mitochondrial biogenesis.

results.result: MitoQ treatment in a BALB/c mouse model of RSV infection significantly reduces viral replication (>4 fold), infectious virus production, bronchial and perivascular inflammation, and systemic RANTES levels from days 4-7 p.i.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C92-C94, C96-C101, C108, and C122 are well-supported by comprehensive in vivo data (Figure 9 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3) including viral load measurements, histological analysis with objective blind scoring, and ELISA for systemic inflammation markers. Statistical significance is properly documented (p<0.001 to p<0.01). The use of primary human bronchial epithelial cells (pBECs) provides additional clinical relevance. The mouse model follows established protocols with appropriate citations.

results.result: RSV infection co-opts host mitochondria through microtubule/dynein-dependent redistribution to favor reduced respiration and enhanced ROS production, which facilitates viral infection. Blocking this process inhibits RSV infection, establishing mitochondria as a viable therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91, C102, C109-C110, and C141 represent integrative conclusions supported by the collective evidence from all experiments. The mechanistic chain from mitochondrial redistribution → respiratory impairment → ROS production → enhanced viral replication is well-established through multiple lines of evidence. The therapeutic potential is demonstrated both in vitro and in vivo. However, some mechanistic details remain unclear, such as how ROS specifically promotes viral replication.

results.result: RSV is responsible for more human deaths each year than influenza and is a leading cause of serious lower respiratory tract illness in infants and a potent respiratory pathogen in elderly and immunosuppressed adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C12 are presented as established facts with citations to Nair et al., 2010 and Hall et al., 2009. However, the claim that RSV causes more deaths than influenza (C1) is stated in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript and may be context-dependent (e.g., specific age groups, geographic regions). The manuscript does not critically evaluate this claim or provide updated epidemiological data. While the citations may support these statements, the accuracy should be verified against current epidemiological evidence.

results.result: There are no effective anti-RSV therapeutics generally available, with palivizumab and ribavirin being the only approved agents as prophylactic and therapeutic, respectively, for high-risk patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 are presented as current facts with citations to papers from 1990-2017. However, the therapeutic landscape for RSV may have changed since publication (2019), and the manuscript does not acknowledge limitations or recent developments. The statement about 'no effective therapeutics' is somewhat contradicted by the existence of approved agents. This contextual information is important for framing the study but may require updating.

results.result: Background claims about RSV biology, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, and prior therapeutic studies are presented with appropriate citations to establish context for the current work.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22, C50, C72, C111-C115, C117-C118, and C123 represent background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide necessary context but are not primary findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the statements are consistent with established knowledge in the field. However, the accuracy of cited work is assumed rather than independently verified.

results.result: The Golgi apparatus remains asymmetrically close to nuclei in both mock- and RSV-infected cells, serving as a specificity control for mitochondrial effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing that Golgi distribution is unchanged by RSV infection, in contrast to mitochondrial redistribution. This serves as an important negative control demonstrating specificity of the mitochondrial effects. However, the manuscript does not quantify Golgi distribution as rigorously as mitochondrial distribution.

results.result: MitoQ does not alter syncytia formation at 48 h p.i., suggesting that mitochondrial ROS facilitates viral replication rather than cell-to-cell spread through fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by quantification of syncytia density and size (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) showing no significant effect of MitoQ treatment. This helps distinguish between effects on viral replication versus spread. However, the interpretation assumes that syncytia formation is the primary mechanism of cell-to-cell spread, which may not be fully accurate for RSV.

results.result: Drug and siRNA treatments affecting RSV virus production do not cause significant cytotoxicity as measured by LDH release, indicating specific effects on mitochondrial distribution/ROS rather than general toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by LDH release assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) showing no significant increase in cell death with any treatment. This is an important control demonstrating that antiviral effects are not due to cytotoxicity. However, LDH release is a relatively crude measure of cell viability, and more sensitive assays might detect subtle effects.

results.result: In the BALB/c mouse model, viral replication and infectious virus titres peak at day 5 p.i. and decline rapidly at day 7 p.i., consistent with previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by viral load data (Figure 9A-B) and citations to previous studies (van Schaik et al., 1998; Taylor et al., 1984). This validates the mouse model and provides context for evaluating MitoQ effects. The kinetics are consistent with established RSV infection models.

results.result: The findings suggest that modulation of oxidative stress and mitochondrial ROS production presents an exciting therapeutic possibility for RSV infection, with MitoQ or similar antioxidants as potential anti-RSV agents.
results.evaluation: Claims C116, C119, C124-C125 represent forward-looking conclusions based on the study's findings and prior literature. These are appropriately framed as implications and possibilities rather than established facts. The safety data for MitoQ from clinical trials (C123) supports the translational potential. However, these remain speculative until clinical trials are conducted for RSV specifically.

results.result: The mechanism by which elevated ROS contributes to RSV infection may relate to nuclear ROS impacting host nuclear gene transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are speculative, based on observation of nuclear ROS (Figure 7D) and citations to proteomic studies showing transcriptional changes. While the spatial observation of nuclear ROS is supported, the mechanistic link to transcriptional regulation is not directly tested in this study. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future investigation but is not demonstrated by the current data.
